Q203681.title: Battle of Pharsalus
paras: Civil war broke out in early 49 BC when Julius Caesar, the conqueror of Gaul, who had been refused permission to stand for the consulship, crossed the Rubicon into Italy. His rival Pompey the Great took the side of the Senate but withdrew to the east. In January 48 Caesar crossed the Adriatic with seven legions, and for months the two armies faced each other in fortified lines around Dyrrhachium (Durrës, in modern Albania). In July Caesar's army was defeated there, and he marched inland across the Pindus mountains into Greece; Pompey followed, and many senators in his camp pressed him to fight.

The armies met near Pharsalus on 9 August 48 BC. In Caesar's own account Pompey had 110 cohorts, about 45,000 men, and a large cavalry force under Titus Labienus massed on his left wing; Caesar had 80 cohorts, about 22,000 men. Foreseeing that Pompey's cavalry would try to ride round his right flank, Caesar took one cohort from each legion of his third line and formed a fourth line behind his right. Pompey ordered his infantry to stand and receive the charge, hoping Caesar's men would arrive exhausted; Caesar's veterans halted halfway to regain their breath before attacking.

When Pompey's cavalry charged and pushed back Caesar's horsemen, the hidden fourth line rushed out and put it to flight, cut down the archers and slingers, and fell on the rear of Pompey's left wing. Caesar then sent in his fresh third line and Pompey's army broke. Pompey left the field for his camp in despair, and when Caesar's troops stormed it he fled to the coast with a few companions. The next day the remnants of his army surrendered and Caesar pardoned them.

The losses are disputed. Caesar claimed that about 15,000 of Pompey's men fell and more than 24,000 were captured, against his own loss of 200 soldiers and some 30 centurions; Plutarch cites Asinius Pollio, who fought for Caesar, for only 6,000 dead. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered as he came ashore. Pharsalus broke the senatorial cause and opened the way to Caesar's sole rule, which historians such as Jona Lendering see as the end of the Roman Republic.

Q169401.title: Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty
paras: In the mid-1970s the Soviet Union began deploying SS-20 missiles, mobile intermediate-range missiles carrying several nuclear warheads each and able to strike Western Europe. In 1979 NATO answered with a 'dual-track' decision: it would seek arms-control talks while deploying American Pershing II and ground-launched cruise missiles in Europe to offset the SS-20s. Negotiations stalled repeatedly in the early 1980s while the deployments went ahead.

Progress came after Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985. The talks widened in 1986 to cover all American and Soviet intermediate-range missiles worldwide, and on 8 December 1987 President Ronald Reagan and Gorbachev signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty. It entered into force on 1 June 1988.

The treaty obliged both countries to eliminate, and never again possess, all ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres, whether nuclear or conventional. It was the first time the superpowers had agreed to reduce their nuclear arsenals and to abolish an entire class of nuclear weapons, and it introduced extensive on-site inspections. By the deadline of 1 June 1991 they had destroyed 2,692 missiles, 1,846 Soviet and 846 American. After the Soviet Union broke up, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Ukraine also became parties.

From 2014 the United States accused Russia of developing and then deploying a banned ground-launched cruise missile, the 9M729 (SSC-8), which Russia denied; NATO allies backed the American finding of a 'material breach' in December 2018. In early February 2019 the United States suspended its obligations (on 1 February according to NATO, 2 February according to the Arms Control Association) and gave six months' notice of withdrawal; Russia also suspended its obligations. The treaty ended on 2 August 2019.

Q541191.title: Anglo-Irish Treaty
paras: The Irish War of Independence began on 21 January 1919, the day the revolutionary parliament, Dáil Éireann, first met and declared independence, with an attack on police at Soloheadbeg in County Tipperary. Irish forces waged a guerrilla war while the Dáil built up its own system of government to undermine British rule, and the fighting grew more intense until a truce on 11 July 1921. Peace talks followed between a British team led by Prime Minister David Lloyd George, with Winston Churchill, Austen Chamberlain and Lord Birkenhead, and an Irish delegation led by Arthur Griffith and including Michael Collins, but not the President of the Dáil, Éamon de Valera.

The Irish aimed for 'external association': a self-governing Ireland with a republican form of government, linked to the British Commonwealth but recognising the Crown only as a symbol. Lloyd George insisted on the Crown and on Ireland's membership of the Commonwealth, and he steered Griffith into accepting a Boundary Commission to settle the border with Northern Ireland instead of a guarantee of Irish unity. Warned by Lloyd George that refusal would mean renewed war within days, the Irish delegates signed the Treaty on 6 December 1921.

The Treaty created the Irish Free State as a dominion of the Commonwealth, with a status like that of Canada or Australia. British forces would leave most of Ireland, but members of the new parliament would swear an oath of allegiance, the British navy kept the use of several ports, and Northern Ireland could, and did, choose to stay out of the new state.

De Valera and the Treaty's opponents called it a betrayal of the Republic, signed under duress. After a bitter debate from 14 December, the Dáil approved it on 7 January 1922 by 64 votes to 57; de Valera led his supporters out in protest, and the formal ratification required by the Treaty followed on 14 January without them. Michael Collins became chairman of a Provisional Government that began building the Free State, but the split over the Treaty led to the Irish Civil War, which broke out about six months later.

Q130754.title: 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami
paras: On the morning of 26 December 2004 a massive earthquake struck under the sea off the west coast of Sumatra, Indonesia. It happened on the subduction zone where the India Plate is pushed beneath the Burma microplate: the fault ruptured from near the epicentre northward as far as the Andaman Islands. The U.S. Geological Survey gives its magnitude as 9.1, though its size and complexity made a precise figure hard to fix. The sudden thrust of the sea floor lifted a huge mass of water and set off a tsunami across the whole Indian Ocean.

The waves reached the coast of Aceh, at the northern tip of Sumatra, within about twenty minutes. The USGS records local run-ups of nearly 32 metres, among the highest ever measured. In Banda Aceh, the largest city of the province, about a quarter of the population died, according to National Geographic. Racing across the ocean at hundreds of miles an hour, the waves struck Thailand, Sri Lanka and India about two hours after the earthquake and reached the coast of Africa hours later. In Sri Lanka the tsunami overturned a crowded train, the worst rail disaster in history.

The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning system, and tsunamis had been rare there, so most people had no warning. National Geographic puts the death toll at more than 225,000, mainly in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India and Thailand; thousands of foreign tourists on winter holiday were among the dead. Some 1.8 million people were displaced.

The world responded with a large relief effort; a United Nations fund raised billions of dollars, most of which went to Indonesia and Sri Lanka. In 2005 the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission helped set up the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning and Mitigation System to detect tsunamis and alert the coastal countries, and warning systems were later improved in other oceans as well.

Q205887.title: Battle of Carrhae
paras: In 53 BC a Roman army under Marcus Licinius Crassus invaded the Parthian Empire and was destroyed near the town of Carrhae, today Harran in Turkey. Crassus, the richest man in Rome, was one of the three partners of the First Triumvirate with Pompey and Julius Caesar, and he had arranged to govern Syria so that he could make war on Parthia. Rivalry with Pompey, whose military fame outshone his, is usually seen as one of his motives. Caesar wrote from Gaul to encourage him, but others objected: Cicero called it a war without just cause, since Parthia had a treaty with Rome, and the tribune Ateius tried to stop him leaving the city.

King Artavasdes II of Armenia offered Crassus some 10,000 armoured horsemen and 30,000 foot soldiers if he would march through Armenia, but Crassus refused and in the spring of 53 BC advanced straight into Mesopotamia with seven legions, about 4,000 cavalry and about as many light troops. The Parthian king Orodes II split his forces: he took most of them to punish Armenia and sent his general Surena, with an army of horsemen only, against the Romans. An Arab chieftain, Ariamnes, guided Crassus. Plutarch paints him as a Parthian agent who led the Romans into waterless desert, but modern historians doubt this: the route followed the valley of the Balikh river, where there was water and farmland.

Near Carrhae, on 9 June according to the poet Ovid, the Romans met Surena's army. Crassus drew up his men in a hollow square with twelve cohorts on each side and, urged on by his son Publius, attacked at once instead of resting at a stream as his officers advised. The Parthians beat drums and their armoured horsemen threw off the coverings of their armour to show it gleaming; then their mounted archers rode round the square shooting, always withdrawing before the legionaries could reach them, while camels brought them fresh arrows. Crassus sent Publius out with 1,300 horsemen, 1,000 of them Gauls, 500 archers and eight cohorts. The Parthians drew this force away by pretending to flee, then surrounded and destroyed it; Publius had himself killed, and the Parthians showed his head on a spear to his father's army.

The attacks went on until nightfall. With Crassus in despair, his officers Octavius and Cassius led a retreat to Carrhae in the dark, abandoning about 4,000 wounded men, whom the Parthians killed the next morning. Surena then offered a truce, and Crassus, pressed by his men, went to meet him; a struggle broke out over a horse brought for him, and Crassus and his officers were killed. Plutarch puts the Roman losses in the whole campaign at about 20,000 dead and 10,000 taken prisoner. The Parthians also took several of the legions' eagle standards, a deep humiliation for Rome.

Gaius Cassius Longinus led some 10,000 survivors back to Syria and defended the province against later Parthian raids. Orodes, jealous of Surena's success, soon had him put to death. Crassus's death ended the Triumvirate, leaving Pompey and Caesar without a third partner to balance them, which the historian Jona Lendering of Livius.org sees as making their civil war only a matter of time. Rome went on seeking revenge in the east; according to Livius.org, the eagles were finally handed back to Tiberius.

Q1455917.title: Umayyad conquest of Hispania
paras: In 711 a Muslim army from North Africa crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and within a few years overthrew the Visigothic kingdom, which had ruled most of the Iberian Peninsula from Toledo for about 300 years. The invaders served the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I in Damascus. Their leader was Tariq ibn Ziyad, governor of Tangier and, according to the Arabic sources, a Berber, acting for his superior Musa ibn Nusayr, the governor of North Africa. The Visigothic kingdom was divided: the accession of its king, Roderic, was disputed, and there had been civil war. Raiding parties sent across in 710 had come back with tales of rich booty. Very little was written at the time, and much of the later story is legend, so many details are uncertain.

Tariq landed near the rock that still bears his name, Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq, 'Tariq's mountain'), with a force made up mostly of Berbers. Its size is uncertain: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, writing about 150 years later, gives 1,700 men, and a modern account about 1,500. In July 711 Tariq defeated Roderic's larger army, probably near the Guadalete river. The only contemporary account, the Chronicle of 754, says that men who had come with Roderic out of rivalry and hope of the crown fled, and desertion is seen as a main reason for the defeat. Roderic was believed to have been killed, leaving the kingdom without a leader.

Tariq pressed on: Cordoba was taken and he marched to the capital, Toledo. In 712 Musa crossed with about 18,000 mostly Arab troops, took Seville and, after a long resistance, Mérida, and joined Tariq. Together they took Zaragoza and other towns of the Ebro valley and then turned north-west towards León and Galicia. Some towns were stormed, but many surrendered on terms. In 713 the Visigothic count Theodemir of Murcia kept his lands as a client ruler, paying tribute while his Christian subjects kept their faith, and this treaty became a model for others. In 714 the caliph summoned Musa and Tariq to Damascus, and Musa left his son Abd al-Aziz to govern.

From about 717 the new rulers raided across the Pyrenees into Septimania in southern Gaul. Caliph Umar II is said to have thought of giving up the distant province. In the mountains of Asturias Pelagius (Pelayo), a former official of the Visigothic court, defeated a Muslim force at Covadonga, the first serious setback for the conquerors, and a small Christian realm survived in the north. The rest of the peninsula became al-Andalus, under Muslim rule for centuries; the last Muslim state, Granada, fell to Castile and Aragon in 1492.

Q27900.title: Siege of Constantinople (717–718)
paras: In 717–718 the Umayyad Caliphate made its greatest attempt to take Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire. Caliph Sulayman, too ill to lead in person, gave command to his brother Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik. Byzantium was weak: for some twenty years the Arabs had been raiding and occupying its borderlands, and since 695 the throne had changed hands seven times in violent coups. Emperor Anastasius II had repaired the city's walls and stocked food in expectation of a siege. When the Arab armies advanced into Asia Minor in 715–716, Maslama made common cause with the general Leo the Isaurian, who had rebelled; but Leo deceived the Arabs, took the throne himself as Leo III and entered the capital on 25 March 717.

In early summer 717 Maslama crossed the Dardanelles into Thrace and marched on the city, which was protected by the sea and by the massive Theodosian Walls. He reached it in mid-July or mid-August (EBSCO gives 15 August) and shut it off by land with a double siege wall. Numbers are uncertain and the medieval figures are inflated: EBSCO gives 80,000 men, the Arab writer al-Mas'udi 120,000, and the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes 1,800 ships; the defenders probably numbered no more than about 15,000. The Arab fleet arrived on 1 September, but as its rearguard of twenty heavy ships passed the city the wind dropped, and the Byzantines attacked them with Greek fire, burning or sinking them. The rest of the fleet would not risk battle, so the city could still be supplied by sea.

The winter was exceptionally hard, with snow on the ground for about three months. Famine broke out in the Arab camp; the soldiers ate their horses and camels and even the bark of trees. In spring 718 the new caliph, Umar II, sent two supply fleets from Egypt and North Africa and a fresh army through Asia Minor. Many of the fleets' sailors were Christian Egyptians who deserted and told Leo where the ships lay; his fleet then destroyed or captured them with Greek fire. The relief army was ambushed and destroyed south of Nicomedia, and the Bulgars, who had a treaty with Leo, attacked the besiegers; Theophanes says they killed 22,000.

Umar ordered a retreat, and on 15 August 718 the Arabs left. It was the feast of the Dormition of the Virgin Mary, and the Byzantines credited her with their victory. Storms and other disasters destroyed most of the returning fleet; Theophanes says only five ships reached Syria. The defeat strained the Umayyad state, and the Caliphate gave up the aim of conquering Constantinople: the frontier settled along the Taurus and Antitaurus mountains, with regular raids but no great change for more than two centuries. The siege is counted among the most important in history, since its failure preserved the Byzantine Empire and delayed a Muslim advance into south-eastern Europe for centuries.

Q492415.title: Battle of Talas
paras: In the summer of 751 the armies of two expanding empires, the Abbasid Caliphate and Tang China, met near the Talas River, on the border of today's Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. It was the only battle ever fought between China and the caliphate. Both sides were reaching into Central Asia for control of the rich lands around the Syr Darya and of a stretch of the Silk Road. The Tang commander was Gao Xianzhi, a general of Korean origin who had already crossed the Pamirs and taken Gilgit from Tibet's allies; the Abbasid army was led by Ziyad ibn Salih, sent by Abu Muslim, the Abbasid governor of Khurasan. The Abbasids had overthrown the Umayyad dynasty only the year before.

The clash grew out of a local quarrel. When the ruler of Ferghana appealed to China against his rival in Shash (modern Tashkent), Gao took Shash, plundered it and had its king executed. The king's son fled to the Abbasids for help, and Ziyad marched east with a large army. The size of the armies is uncertain: each side's sources give the enemy 100,000 or 200,000 men, which historians regard as exaggerations. Chinese sources put the Tang force at about 30,000, including allied troops, and it also had a contingent of Karluk (Qarluq) Turks.

According to the Chinese accounts the battle lasted five days. For several days archers and infantry fought in the centre, with neither side breaking through. Then the Karluks attacked the Tang army from the rear while the Abbasids struck from the front, and it collapsed. Gao and some of his officers escaped, but most of his troops were killed or captured. The sources differ on whether the Karluks changed sides during the battle or had been allied to the Abbasids from the start.

The victory confirmed Abbasid control of Transoxiana and marked the end of Tang expansion to the west, though historians disagree on how much it changed: relations between the two empires soon returned to normal, and in 755 the An Lushan rebellion forced China to withdraw its troops from Central Asia in any case. Over the following centuries Central Asia gradually became Muslim. Chinese prisoners taken at Talas are traditionally said to have brought papermaking to the Islamic world; Medievalists.net presents this as fact, while Wikipedia, citing Jonathan Bloom, notes that paper was already used and probably made in Samarkand decades before the battle. One prisoner, Du Huan, spent years in the caliphate and later wrote an account of his travels.

Q332543.title: Battle of the Pyramids
paras: On 21 July 1798 a French army under General Napoleon Bonaparte defeated the Mamluk forces of Egypt near the village of Embabeh, on the west bank of the Nile across from Cairo. Egypt belonged to the Ottoman Empire but was in practice run by the Mamluk beys, above all Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey. Bonaparte had proposed the expedition to the French government, the Directory, in place of an invasion of Britain; holding Egypt was meant to threaten Britain's route to India. The French landed and stormed Alexandria on 2 July, then marched up the Nile towards Cairo through great heat and thirst, beating off a Mamluk attack at Shubra Khit on 13 July.

Murad Bey chose to fight on the west bank, with his right resting on the fortified village of Embabeh and the Nile, while Ibrahim Bey's army stayed on the east bank and could not join in. His strength lay in several thousand richly armed Mamluk horsemen, supported by peasant infantry and cannon. Bonaparte formed his five divisions into large hollow squares, with infantry ranks on every side, artillery at the corners and his few cavalry and the baggage inside, and advanced with the Nile on his left. Before the battle he told his men that forty centuries looked down on them from the pyramids, which stood some miles away.

In the afternoon the Mamluk cavalry charged the squares on the French right, the divisions of Desaix and Reynier, again and again. The French infantry held their fire until the horsemen were almost upon them and cut them down with musketry and cannon. Near the river, the divisions of Bon and Vial then stormed Embabeh. Its defenders broke, and many tried to escape across the Nile, where hundreds drowned. Murad, wounded in the face, got away with part of his cavalry and withdrew to Upper Egypt, while Ibrahim abandoned Cairo and retreated towards Syria.

Losses were very unequal. The French officially reported 29 dead, with the wounded given as 120 or 260; the Mamluk side lost thousands, with estimates ranging from about 2,000 Mamluks plus several thousand peasant soldiers to as many as 10,000. Bonaparte entered Cairo on 24 July and set up a French administration there. The victory began the end of centuries of Mamluk power in Egypt, but its strategic value was short-lived: ten days later Nelson's fleet destroyed the French fleet at the Battle of the Nile, cutting the army off from France.

Q243979.title: Battle of the Nile
paras: On 1–3 August 1798 a British fleet under Rear-Admiral Horatio Nelson destroyed the French Mediterranean fleet at anchor in Aboukir Bay, on the Egyptian coast east of Alexandria. The French fleet, under Vice-Admiral François-Paul Brueys, had sailed from Toulon in May carrying General Bonaparte's army to Egypt, capturing Malta on the way; the expedition was meant as a first step against British India. Nelson chased the French across the Mediterranean for more than two months, missing them more than once, and the army landed in Egypt unopposed.

With the army ashore, Brueys anchored his thirteen ships of the line in a line across Aboukir Bay, with his huge flagship L'Orient in the centre, believing the position strong. Many of his sailors were ashore finding supplies, and he had no scouts out. On the afternoon of 1 August a British lookout sighted the French, and Nelson, with thirteen ships of the line of his own, attacked at once, though evening was coming on. Captain Thomas Foley of Goliath saw room to pass round the head of the French line, and he and several others sailed between the anchored French ships and the shore, while Nelson and the rest attacked from the seaward side. The leading French ships, caught between two fires, were battered into surrender one by one.

In the centre, L'Orient caught fire and at about 10 p.m. blew up, killing most of her crew. Brueys was also killed: Wikipedia says by a cannonball shortly before, while Royal Museums Greenwich counts him among the explosion's victims. The shock stopped the firing for some minutes. Fighting went on through the night and the next morning, but the French rear division under Villeneuve did little to help, and only two French ships of the line and two frigates escaped. The British lost 218 killed and about 677 wounded, Nelson among the wounded, hit in the head. French losses are estimated at 2,000 to 5,000.

The victory reversed the balance of power in the Mediterranean and gave the Royal Navy a control of the sea it kept for the rest of the war. Bonaparte's army was cut off in Egypt. The battle encouraged the Ottoman Empire to declare war on France and helped bring Austria and Russia into the Second Coalition. Nelson was made a baron and hailed as a hero across Europe.

Q154426.title: Battle of Jena–Auerstedt
paras: On 14 October 1806 Napoleon's Grande Armée destroyed the army of Prussia and its Saxon allies in two battles fought the same day, at Jena and at Auerstedt, further north, in today's Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt. They were the decisive battles of the War of the Fourth Coalition, which Prussia had begun by declaring war on France. Napoleon pushed some 180,000 men through the Franconian Forest towards Saxony and Berlin; the Prussians waited with about 130,000 of their own men and 20,000 Saxons. Their command was divided and slow: key posts were shared among several officers, the main army under the Duke of Brunswick was separated from Prince Hohenlohe's force, and there was little coordination between them.

At Jena, Napoleon attacked Hohenlohe in the morning fog, believing he faced the main Prussian army. The French built up their strength through the day until they far outnumbered the Prussians (Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: 96,000 against 38,000). Marshal Ney attacked without orders and was nearly surrounded; Napoleon sent Lannes to his aid, holding the weakened centre with the Imperial Guard. In the early afternoon Napoleon ordered his flanks forward; the Prussian line broke, and reinforcements under General Rüchel arriving from Weimar were swept away in the rout. The Prussians lost about 10,000 to 11,000 killed and wounded and 15,000 prisoners, the French about 5,000.

The real Prussian main army, about 63,000–64,000 men with King Frederick William III and Brunswick, was meanwhile further north and ran into Marshal Davout's single corps near Auerstedt, which it outnumbered more than two to one (the Encyclopedia of Modern Europe puts Davout's corps at 26,000). Davout's divisions formed squares, beat off the Prussian cavalry under Blücher and held the village of Hassenhausen against repeated attacks. Brunswick was mortally wounded, and when Davout's last division came up he went over to the attack. Shortly after noon the Prussian army broke. Davout's corps lost about 7,000 men killed and wounded, more than a quarter of its strength according to the Encyclopedia of Modern Europe; the Prussians lost some 12,000–13,000. Marshal Bernadotte, close enough to hear both battles, did not come to Davout's help, which caused lasting controversy.

Napoleon at first refused to believe that Davout had beaten the main Prussian army alone, but later made him Duke of Auerstedt. The beaten Prussians collapsed under a ruthless French pursuit; fortresses surrendered, often without a fight, Davout's corps entered Berlin on 25 October, and Napoleon overran Prussia in a matter of weeks. The disaster showed the need for change: officers present at the battle, among them Scharnhorst, Gneisenau and Clausewitz, led the reforms that began Prussia's transformation into a modern state.

Q838980.title: May Revolution
paras: The May Revolution was a week of events in Buenos Aires, capital of the Spanish Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (roughly today's Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay), that ended on 25 May 1810 with the removal of the viceroy and the creation of a local government, the Primera Junta. It was a direct result of Napoleon's invasion of Spain. In 1808 King Ferdinand VII had been forced to give up the throne, and a Supreme Central Junta governed in his name; in 1810 the French overran Andalusia, and the Junta fell and was replaced by a Council of Regency in Cádiz. When the news reached Buenos Aires in May, criollos (Spaniards born in the Americas) argued that the authority which had appointed Viceroy Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros no longer existed.

On 18 May Cisneros issued a proclamation calling for loyalty to Ferdinand VII, but it only fed the unrest. Criollo leaders meeting at the house of Nicolás Rodríguez Peña sent Juan José Castelli and Martín Rodríguez to demand an open cabildo, a special assembly of leading citizens. When Cisneros called the military commanders to the fort, Colonel Cornelio Saavedra of the Patricios regiment refused him support, and the viceroy gave way. On 21 May some 600 armed men led by Domingo French and Antonio Beruti filled the main square, the Plaza de la Victoria (today's Plaza de Mayo), demanding the assembly; they carried portraits of Ferdinand and wore white ribbons as a sign of unity.

The open cabildo met on 22 May. The bishop of Buenos Aires argued that Spaniards should rule as long as a single one remained in America; Castelli answered that with the king's government gone, sovereignty returned to the people, who could form their own government until Ferdinand returned. Juan José Paso argued that Buenos Aires, as an 'elder sister', should act first and invite the other cities to join. The vote went against the viceroy, 155 to 69, and the town council took provisional power. But on 24 May the council named a junta with Cisneros himself as president. Protest grew, and that night Saavedra and Castelli resigned from it and told Cisneros he must step down.

On 25 May, as a crowd gathered in the square and the military commanders refused to act against it, the council gave way. A petition proposing a new junta was accepted, and the Primera Junta took office, with Saavedra as president, Mariano Moreno and Juan José Paso as secretaries, and Manuel Belgrano, Castelli and others as members. It governed in the name of Ferdinand VII, and historians still debate whether that loyalty was sincere or a cover for independence. The revolution began the Argentine War of Independence, and fighting soon broke out with the regions that stayed loyal to Spain; independence was formally declared at the Congress of Tucumán on 9 July 1816. 25 May is a national holiday in Argentina.

Q156681.title: Battle of Sedan
paras: On 1–2 September 1870, early in the Franco-Prussian War, German armies surrounded a French army at the fortress town of Sedan, near the Belgian border, and forced it to surrender together with Emperor Napoleon III. France had declared war on 19 July, after Bismarck's deliberately provocative Ems Dispatch, and the other states of the North German Confederation and the south German states joined Prussia. In August the Prussians won a string of battles, and after Gravelotte on 18 August Marshal Bazaine's Army of the Rhine was shut up in the fortress of Metz.

A new French army, the Army of Châlons, about 130,000 strong under Marshal MacMahon and accompanied by Napoleon III, set out to relieve Metz by a northern route. The chief of the Prussian general staff, Helmuth von Moltke, kept Metz under siege and sent two armies north against it. After a defeat at Beaumont on 30 August, MacMahon fell back to Sedan to rest his tired troops and did not entrench, which gave the Germans time to close the ring. According to the Deutsches Historisches Museum, more than 200,000 German soldiers of the Third Army and the Meuse (Fourth) Army surrounded the French. 'Now we have them in the mousetrap,' Moltke is reported to have said.

Fighting began early on 1 September at the village of Bazeilles, where Bavarian troops met fierce resistance. MacMahon was wounded, and command passed first to General Ducrot, who ordered a retreat, and then to General Wimpffen, who held a commission from Paris to succeed MacMahon and cancelled it. The French made one uncoordinated attempt after another to break out, including three charges by General Margueritte's cavalry, but the Germans held the high ground around the town, where their breech-loading guns, firing from beyond the range of the French artillery, pounded the trapped army. In the afternoon French units began to fall apart, and Napoleon III, who had ridden about the field seemingly looking for death, had a white flag raised and sent a letter of surrender to King Wilhelm I.

On 2 September Wimpffen signed the capitulation. About 104,000 French soldiers went into captivity, along with 558 guns; some 17,000 French had been killed or wounded, against about 9,000–10,000 German casualties. The capture of the emperor brought down the Second Empire: on 4 September Paris proclaimed a Government of National Defence, which became the Third Republic and fought on for five months. German armies went on to besiege Paris, and the war ended with German unification under the Prussian king and France's loss of Alsace and part of Lorraine. Germans celebrated 2 September as 'Sedan Day' until it was officially abolished in 1919.

Q158021.title: Treaty of Frankfurt
paras: The Treaty of Frankfurt, signed at Frankfurt am Main on 10 May 1871 between the new German Empire and the French Third Republic, ended the Franco-Prussian War. France had declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870 and had been defeated: its emperor, Napoleon III, was captured at Sedan in September, the republic that replaced him could not break the siege of Paris, and the city capitulated on 28 January 1871, when an armistice was signed. On 18 January, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the Prussian king Wilhelm I had been proclaimed emperor of a united Germany. A preliminary peace was signed at Versailles on 26 February by Otto von Bismarck and the French leader Adolphe Thiers, and the Frankfurt treaty confirmed it.

Under the treaty France gave up Alsace, except the city of Belfort and its territory, and most of the department of Moselle and other parts of Lorraine, including the city of Metz. France lost about 1.6 million inhabitants and some 1,694 towns and villages. People in the annexed lands could choose to keep French nationality and move to France, and about a tenth of the population did so, according to the Deutsches Historisches Museum. France also had to pay a war indemnity of five billion francs, and German troops occupied parts of the country until it was paid; France paid ahead of schedule, and the last troops left in September 1873. The treaty also recognised Wilhelm I as German Emperor.

The German army wanted the new border for security, above all the route between Thionville and Metz, while nationalists argued that the region had once belonged to the Holy Roman Empire and mostly spoke German dialects. The loss of French-speaking areas such as Metz caused outrage in France. The annexed lands became the 'Reichsland' of Alsace-Lorraine, governed directly under the Kaiser. Recovering the 'lost provinces' became a central aim of French policy for the next forty years and one of the strongest French motives in the First World War; Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France by the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.

Q302519.title: Battle of Adwa
paras: On 1 March 1896, near the town of Adwa in northern Ethiopia, the army of Emperor Menelik II destroyed an Italian colonial army under General Oreste Baratieri, the decisive battle of the First Italo-Ethiopian War. The quarrel went back to the Treaty of Wuchale (Wichale), signed in 1889. Its Italian text said that Ethiopia must conduct its foreign affairs through Italy, which made it in effect an Italian protectorate; the Amharic text said only that the emperor could use Italy's good offices if he wished. Italy's prime minister, Francesco Crispi, declared a protectorate, Menelik rejected it, and Italy turned to force.

Italian troops from the colony of Eritrea advanced into Tigray in 1895, but Menelik called his whole country to arms, and his vanguard wiped out an Italian unit at Amba Alagi in December. His army, largely armed with modern rifles bought from abroad, numbered somewhere between 73,000 and over 100,000 men; the Italian force at Adwa was much smaller, about 15,000 to 20,000 men. By late February both sides were short of supplies. Baratieri thought of retreating, but Rome was pressing him to act and his brigadiers argued for an attack, so on the night of 29 February he sent three brigades forward with a fourth in reserve, hoping to surprise the Ethiopians in their camp.

The plan fell apart in the dark, over rough ground and with poor maps. General Albertone's brigade, of Eritrean askaris, went the wrong way and found itself cut off well ahead of the others, and General Dabormida's brigade, sent to help it, drifted into a separate valley, leaving a wide gap. The Ethiopians attacked each column in turn. Albertone's brigade was overrun; Menelik committed his reserve, and the Italian centre under General Arimondi, outflanked on both sides, broke around midday. Baratieri ordered a retreat that turned into a rout, pursued by Oromo cavalry, and Dabormida's isolated brigade was surrounded and destroyed later in the day.

Italian losses were heavy: Wikipedia's figures give some 6,000 dead and about 3,800 taken prisoner, while EBSCO gives about 7,000 dead, 1,500 wounded and some 3,000 prisoners. Ethiopian losses were also high, estimated at roughly 4,000 to 7,000 killed. The Italians left behind all their artillery and thousands of rifles. Menelik did not pursue them into Eritrea, but the defeat brought down Crispi's government, and in the Treaty of Addis Ababa Italy recognised Ethiopia's full independence. Ethiopia remained one of the very few independent states in Africa, and Adwa became a symbol of resistance for Africans under colonial rule; for many Italians it became a humiliation to be avenged, which Mussolini's invasion of 1935 claimed to do.

Q164771.title: Agadir Crisis
paras: The Agadir Crisis, or Second Moroccan Crisis, of 1911 began when Germany sent the gunboat Panther to the Moroccan Atlantic port of Agadir on 1 July 1911. After the first Moroccan crisis, the Algeciras conference of 1906 and a Franco-German agreement of 9 February 1909 had recognised France's political lead in Morocco while protecting Germany's economic interests. In the spring of 1911, with Sultan Abd al-Hafid facing a revolt, France sent troops deep into the country, occupying Fez on the pretext of protecting Europeans. Germany saw this as a breach of the earlier agreements.

The German foreign secretary, Alfred von Kiderlen-Wächter, was prepared to let France have Morocco, but only in return for territorial compensation, above all the French Congo. The Panther, officially sent to protect German trade, was meant to force France to negotiate. In mid-July Germany formally demanded the French Congo, and the German nationalist press stirred up a warlike mood. Britain, tied to France by the Entente Cordiale and alarmed at the prospect of a German naval base on the Atlantic, took France's side. On 21 July David Lloyd George, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, warned in his Mansion House speech that peace bought by letting Britain be treated as of no account would be an intolerable humiliation. Germany took the speech as a warning, and it caused anger there.

Germany's leaders were ready to threaten war but did not want one, and a financial panic in Germany added to the pressure on Berlin to settle. In an agreement signed on 4 November 1911, Germany accepted French control of Morocco, keeping only guarantees for its economic interests, and in return received about 275,000 square kilometres of the French Congo, added to its colony of Kamerun, while ceding a smaller area to France. Many in Germany saw the result as a diplomatic defeat, and nationalists complained that Germany had gained too little.

The crisis drew Britain and France closer and deepened Anglo-German hostility; it led to an Anglo-French naval agreement, under which the Royal Navy was to guard France's northern coast while the French fleet concentrated in the Mediterranean. In Germany calls for a preventive war grew, and in France anti-German feeling revived. In March 1912 the Treaty of Fes made Morocco a French protectorate, which lasted until 1956.

Q468823.title: March on Rome
paras: The March on Rome of 27–28 October 1922 was the Fascist mobilisation that brought Benito Mussolini to power in Italy. Mussolini had founded his Fasci di Combattimento in Milan in 1919, during the 'Red Biennium' of strikes and factory and land occupations. His armed squads, the Blackshirts, attacked socialists, trade unions, cooperatives and left-wing newspapers, often with the backing of landowners and industrialists and with little interference from the police. In 1921 the Fascists won 35 seats in parliament on Giovanni Giolitti's lists, and the movement became the National Fascist Party; in August 1922 its squads broke an anti-fascist general strike and drove the socialist administration out of Milan's town hall.

Mussolini combined threats of insurrection with talks with liberal leaders about joining a government. On 24 October, at a rally in Naples, he declared that the Fascist programme was simply to rule Italy, and four leaders, the 'quadrumvirs' Emilio De Bono, Italo Balbo, Michele Bianchi and Cesare Maria De Vecchi, were put in charge of the march while he stayed in Milan. Fascist squads occupied prefectures, post offices and stations in towns of northern and central Italy, and columns of poorly armed Blackshirts gathered outside Rome.

On the morning of 28 October the government of Luigi Facta, which had already resigned, approved a state of siege, but King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign the decree. His reasons have never been fully explained; doubts about the army's loyalty, fear of civil war and the ambitions of his pro-Fascist cousin, the Duke of Aosta, have all been suggested. The army in Rome could easily have stopped the squads, but no clash took place. On 29 October the king invited Mussolini to form a government; Mussolini took the night train from Milan, arrived on the 30th, and on 31 October formed a coalition cabinet while the Blackshirts paraded through the city.

Mussolini thus came to power legally, under the constitution, through the surrender of the authorities to Fascist intimidation rather than by a seizure of power, although the Fascists later celebrated the march as a conquest of power. Fascist squads attacked opponents in Rome's working-class districts, and according to Il Post about 22 people died in the following days. Over the next few years, especially after the murder of the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti in 1924, Mussolini turned his government into a dictatorship.

Q152925.title: Locarno Treaties
paras: The Locarno Treaties were a set of agreements negotiated at Locarno, on Lake Maggiore in southern Switzerland, in October 1925 and formally signed in London on 1 December 1925. Their aim was to bring security to western Europe after the First World War. Germany resented the Treaty of Versailles and wanted it revised, while France, Belgium, Poland and Czechoslovakia feared a revival of German power and wanted their borders guaranteed. Two attempts to build security through the League of Nations, in 1923 and 1924, had failed after Britain rejected them.

In February 1925 the German foreign minister, Gustav Stresemann, proposed a guarantee of the Franco-German frontier and of the demilitarised zone in the Rhineland. The British foreign secretary, Austen Chamberlain, after some hesitation, backed the idea as a way to calm French fears, and the French foreign minister, Aristide Briand, took part in the talks. The delegations of Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Belgium, Poland and Czechoslovakia met at Locarno in October, and on 16 October the agreements were completed at the town hall.

The most important treaty, the Rhineland Pact, was a mutual guarantee between Germany, France, Belgium, Britain and Italy. Germany accepted its borders with France and Belgium and the demilitarised zone along the Rhine; Germany, France and Belgium promised not to go to war with one another except in self-defence or League action and to settle disputes by arbitration; and Britain and Italy undertook to act against any violation. In the east, Stresemann would not guarantee Germany's borders: Germany signed only arbitration treaties with Poland and Czechoslovakia, and France made new mutual-assistance treaties with those two countries. The treaties took effect once Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926.

Locarno was hailed as the start of a 'Great Peace', and for the first time since the war Germany was treated as a respected power. All three foreign ministers received the Nobel Peace Prize: according to the Foreign Office historians, Chamberlain shared the prize for 1925 and Stresemann and Briand the prize for 1926. But the 'spirit of Locarno' did not last. Poland and Czechoslovakia were left without a German guarantee of their frontiers, critics later saw the treaties as encouraging German ambitions in the east, and with the Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed the optimism faded; Germany under Hitler eventually broke the agreements.

Q153376.title: Second Battle of El Alamein
paras: The Second Battle of El Alamein, fought near Egypt's western frontier from 23 October to 4 November 1942, was the turning point of the North African campaign of the Second World War. The British Eighth Army defeated the German and Italian army of Field Marshal Erwin Rommel. Since 1940 the war in the desert had swung back and forth, and in 1942 Rommel defeated the British at Gazala, took Tobruk and drove them back into Egypt, threatening the Suez Canal. The British made their stand at El Alamein, a short front between the Mediterranean and the impassable Qattara Depression that could not be outflanked, and in the summer they stopped Rommel's last attempts to break through.

In the summer of 1942 Lieutenant-General Bernard Montgomery took command of the Eighth Army. Resisting Churchill's pressure for an early attack, he built up a force of more than 190,000 men from across the British Empire and from Greece, Poland and France, with over 1,000 tanks. The Axis army was short of fuel, partly because British codebreakers reading German Enigma traffic helped sink most of its supply ships, so Rommel dug in behind deep minefields he called the 'devil's gardens'. When the battle began, Rommel was on sick leave in Germany; he hurried back to take command.

Montgomery opened the offensive on the night of 23 October with a massive artillery barrage. In Operation Lightfoot, infantry and engineers cleared two corridors through the minefields for the armour, and then began a grinding battle of attrition. British tanks were held up in the crowded corridors and lost heavily to anti-tank guns, but Axis counter-attacks were beaten off. After pausing to regroup, Montgomery launched his final attack, Operation Supercharge, at the beginning of November. Rommel began to withdraw, but Hitler ordered the position held at all costs; by 4 November the Axis army was broken and in retreat. Many Axis tanks and much of the infantry without motor transport were lost, though Montgomery's caution allowed the motorised units to escape.

El Alamein was the British Army's first clear and lasting victory over the Axis and a great boost to British morale. On 8 November Anglo-American forces landed in Algeria and Morocco in Operation Torch, leaving the Axis fighting on two fronts in North Africa; Montgomery pursued Rommel back through Libya into Tunisia, where the Axis armies surrendered in May 1943. Churchill called it 'the end of the beginning'. Its strategic weight is debated, since North Africa was small compared with the Eastern Front, but the battle made Montgomery's reputation.

Q696835.title: Liberation of Paris
paras: Paris had been under German occupation for four years. After the Allied landings in Normandy and the breakout from the beachhead in the summer of 1944, the Allied commanders, Eisenhower and Bradley, planned to bypass the city and encircle it rather than spend troops and supplies on a costly fight for it and on feeding its population. Inside Paris the Resistance had other ideas. Strikes spread through the city in August, and the communist Colonel Henri Rol-Tanguy, regional head of the French Forces of the Interior (FFI), called the population to arms. General de Gaulle and his supporters also wanted Frenchmen to free their own capital, to assert French sovereignty and avoid an Allied military administration, though they worried that a rising would come too early.

The uprising began on 19 August. Resistance policemen seized the Prefecture of Police on the Île de la Cité and raised the tricolour, and Resistance fighters took the Hôtel de Ville. Through the Swedish consul, Raoul Nordling, a truce was arranged with the German commander, General Dietrich von Choltitz, but it was only partly observed. Rol-Tanguy, directing the fight from an underground command post at Place Denfert-Rochereau, ordered barricades built, and Parisians tore up paving stones to raise hundreds of them across the city. The lightly armed insurgents faced a German garrison of many thousands with tanks and armoured vehicles. Hitler had ordered that Paris should fall only as a field of ruins; Choltitz had bridges and some major buildings mined, but did not give the order to destroy them.

De Gaulle pressed Eisenhower to send troops into the city and warned that otherwise he would send in General Leclerc's French 2nd Armoured Division himself. Eisenhower agreed, and the French division and the U.S. 4th Infantry Division advanced on Paris. After hard fighting on the approaches, Leclerc's first units reached the Hôtel de Ville late at night. On 25 August German resistance collapsed; in the afternoon Choltitz surrendered. Leclerc received the capitulation at the Gare Montparnasse, where he had his headquarters; signed by Choltitz and countersigned by Rol-Tanguy, it surrendered Paris to de Gaulle's provisional government.

De Gaulle arrived the same afternoon and spoke at the Hôtel de Ville to a jubilant crowd: 'Paris martyred! But Paris liberated!' On 26 August he led a triumphal march down the Champs-Élysées, disturbed by scattered shots from rooftops. The losses among fighters and civilians are given by Hérodote as anything from a few hundred to more than three thousand. The liberation of the capital by the French themselves restored French confidence and established de Gaulle's provisional government in Paris.

Q482407.title: Geneva Conference of 1954
paras: The Geneva Conference met at the Palace of Nations in Geneva from 26 April to 21 July 1954 to settle questions left open by two wars: the Korean War, ended by an armistice the year before, and the First Indochina War between France and the communist-led Viet Minh. At the Berlin Conference in February 1954 the participants had agreed that peace in Indochina would also be discussed at the planned conference on Korea. Korea came first on the agenda.

The Korean talks, from 26 April to 15 June, brought together South Korea, North Korea, China, the Soviet Union and the United States, along with other allied delegations such as those of Britain and Belgium. South Korea held that its government was the only legal one in Korea and wanted UN-supervised elections in the North and the withdrawal of Chinese troops. North Korea proposed all-Korean elections after all foreign forces had left, run by a commission drawn equally from North and South; China suggested supervision by neutral nations, which the North accepted, while the United States backed the South. On 15 June, the last day of the Korean talks, the Soviet Union and China put forward declarations in favour of a unified Korea, but the participants agreed on no declaration, and the Korean part of the conference ended without result.

The Indochina talks began on 8 May, the day after the French garrison at Dien Bien Phu fell to the Viet Minh. Taking part were France, Britain, the United States, the Soviet Union, China, the Viet Minh's Democratic Republic of Vietnam, the rival State of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. The United States had considered air strikes to save Dien Bien Phu but could not win support from allies such as Britain; Secretary of State John Foster Dulles refused any contact with the Chinese delegation led by Zhou Enlai and left Geneva on 3 May. In June a new French prime minister, Pierre Mendès France, pledged to resign if he did not reach a ceasefire within 30 days, and Zhou, meeting Ho Chi Minh in early July, urged the Viet Minh to accept a compromise to keep the United States from intervening.

The agreements were dated 20 July but signed on the morning of 21 July. They ended the fighting in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia and divided Vietnam along a military demarcation line near the 17th parallel: Viet Minh forces were to regroup to the north and French and State of Vietnam forces to the south, and for 300 days people could move freely between the zones. A commission of India, Canada and Poland was to supervise the ceasefire. A Final Declaration stated that the line was provisional and not a political or territorial boundary, and that general elections would be held in July 1956 under international supervision. The United States and the State of Vietnam did not accept the declaration. Wikipedia counts three ceasefire agreements plus the declaration; the U.S. State Department's summary speaks of two agreements.

Historians generally see the conference as having failed to bring lasting peace to Indochina. France withdrew from the region, the United States became ever more committed to opposing communism there, and the growing hostility between the communist North and the anti-communist South led to the Vietnam War.

Q56039.title: German reunification
paras: German reunification was the process, from the opening of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 to 3 October 1990, by which the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) joined the Federal Republic of Germany. In 1989 a continuing stream of East Germans leaving for the West and mass protests for democratic freedoms put the ruling party, the SED, under growing pressure; after Erich Honecker stepped down, it tried to keep power through concessions. On 9 November 1989 the Politburo member Günter Schabowski unexpectedly announced at a press conference that East Germans could travel out at once and without preconditions. Thousands gathered at the crossings to West Berlin, and that night border guards opened them without clear orders.

On 28 November 1989 the West German chancellor Helmut Kohl surprised his coalition partner and the Western allies with a ten-point programme in the Bundestag that put unity on the agenda: confederal structures between the two states were to lead to a federation, within wider European integration. The Soviet Union, Britain and France reacted with scepticism, fearing a powerful Germany in the middle of Europe. In East Germany, demonstrators now began to call for unity, chanting 'We are one people' instead of 'We are the people'.

The first free election to East Germany's parliament, the Volkskammer, on 18 March 1990, became a vote on unity. The 'Alliance for Germany', led by the eastern CDU and backing quick unification, won about 48 per cent, the SPD 21.9 per cent and the PDS, the renamed SED, about 16 per cent. Lothar de Maizière (CDU) formed a grand coalition to prepare East Germany's accession under Article 23 of West Germany's Basic Law, rather than a new constitution under Article 146. A treaty on monetary, economic and social union took effect on 1 July 1990: the Deutsche Mark became East Germany's only currency, and wages, rents and pensions were converted one to one.

On 23 August 1990 the Volkskammer voted for accession. The Unification Treaty was signed on 31 August by Wolfgang Schäuble for West Germany and Günther Krause for East Germany and approved by both parliaments on 20 September. On 3 October 1990 East Germany joined the Federal Republic as five new states (Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia), Berlin became the capital again, and 3 October became a national holiday.

The external side was settled in 'Two Plus Four' talks between the two German states and the four victors of 1945 (the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France) held by their foreign ministers from May 1990. The United States backed unity on condition that Germany stay in NATO, and Mikhail Gorbachev accepted that a united Germany could choose its alliance. The treaty signed in Moscow on 12 September 1990 kept Germany in NATO, capped its armed forces at 370,000, renewed its renunciation of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons, made its borders, above all with Poland, final, and gave it full sovereignty. Sources differ on when the treaty took effect: deutschland.de gives 15 March 1991, the CVCE 3 October 1990.

Q677316.title: Social War
paras: The Social War (Latin bellum sociale, 'war of the allies'), which Romans of the time called the Marsic or Italian War, was fought in Italy, mainly from 91 to 88 BC, between the Roman Republic and many of its Italian allies (socii). The main rebels were the Marsi, Samnites, Hirpini, Frentani, Vestini, Marrucini, Paeligni and Picentines. Under separate treaties the allied cities kept self-government but had to send men to Rome's wars, and they did not have the rights of Roman citizens. Why they rebelled is debated: the main ancient account, by Appian, centres on a demand for Roman citizenship, while some modern historians, notably Henrik Mouritsen, see a revolt against Roman dominance and encroachment on allied land.

In 91 BC the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus proposed laws granting citizenship to the allies and was murdered. The war began at Asculum, in late 91 BC or early 90 BC, where the townspeople killed a Roman praetor, Quintus Servilius, and all the Romans in the town; other Italian peoples then rose too. The rebels made Corfinium their capital, renamed Italia, with a senate of 500 members and two consuls: Quintus Poppaedius Silo, who led in the north, and Gaius Papius Mutilus in the south.

In 90 BC the rebels did well at first. Mutilus took Nola, Herculaneum and Salernum in Campania, while in Picenum Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo was defeated and shut up in Firmum. On 11 June the consul Publius Rutilius Lupus was killed by the Marsi at the Tolenus river, but Gaius Marius, helped by Lucius Cornelius Sulla, then beat the Marsi near the Fucine Lake and split the rebel territory in two. Late that year a law of the consul Lucius Julius Caesar, the lex Julia, offered Roman citizenship to communities that had not revolted or that laid down their arms, which drained support from the rebellion.

In 89 BC the consul Lucius Porcius Cato was killed fighting the Marsi, but Strabo besieged Asculum, which surrendered in November. In the south Sulla took Pompeii, Stabiae and Herculaneum, subdued the Hirpini and captured Bovianum, which won him the consulship for 88 BC; a further law, the lex Plautia Papiria, extended citizenship again. By 88 BC the war was largely over, and the last Samnite and Lucanian rebels reached a settlement in 87 BC. Wikipedia dates the war 91-87 BC; EBSCO and the Columbia Encyclopedia give 91-88 BC.

The war ended with Roman citizenship extended to the peoples of Italy. How the new citizens were to be enrolled in the Roman voting tribes remained a bitter question and played a part in Sulla's march on Rome in 88 BC. Because it also put large armies under ambitious generals inside Italy, some historians see the war as an important step towards the fall of the Roman Republic.

Q335330.title: Battle of Philippi
paras: The Battle of Philippi, in Macedonia in 42 BC, was in fact two battles between the armies of Julius Caesar's assassins and of his avengers. After the murder of Caesar in 44 BC, Brutus took control of Macedonia and was joined there by Cassius, who held Syria. Caesar's friend Mark Antony and his heir Octavian, the future emperor Augustus, settled their quarrel in 43 BC and with Marcus Aemilius Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate; in 42 BC Antony and Octavian marched east to retake the eastern provinces. Brutus and Cassius held two hills west of Philippi on the Via Egnatia, supplied from Neapolis, while the triumvirs drew their supplies from more distant Amphipolis. The ancient historian Appian gives each side nineteen legions, the republicans' not quite full; EBSCO's account gives the triumvirs twenty-eight legions to the republicans' nineteen.

In the first battle Antony tried to cut his enemies' communications by building a causeway through the marshes south of the town, and Cassius answered with a dam across its path. Antony then suddenly stormed Cassius's camp and took it. At the same time Brutus's men routed Octavian's army and captured the triumvirs' camp, though Octavian escaped. Cassius, believing all was lost and not knowing of Brutus's success, killed himself. Each side had won one victory and suffered one defeat.

The triumvirs were soon short of food: Thessaly could no longer feed them, the republicans controlled the sea, the triumvirs had just suffered a naval disaster in the Adriatic, and winter was coming. Brutus wanted to wait until hunger wore them down, but his soldiers and officers demanded battle, and he gave way. In the second battle, on 23 October, the armies fought at close quarters until Octavian's troops forced Brutus's line back; it broke, the fugitives were cut off from their camp, and Antony's cavalry hunted down those who escaped. Brutus spent the night in the hills with fewer than four legions; the next day his officers refused to fight on, and he took his own life.

Philippi ended the cause of Caesar's assassins and confirmed the power of the triumvirs. Later Octavian defeated Antony at Actium and became sole ruler of the Roman world as Augustus, so that the battle came to mark a step in the Roman Republic's turn into a monarchy.

Q159512.title: Battle of Legnica
paras: The Battle of Legnica (in German, Liegnitz) was fought on 9 April 1241 in Silesia between a Mongol army and the forces of Duke Henry II the Pious of Silesia. In 1241 the Mongol commander Batu Khan made the kingdom of Hungary the main target of his invasion of Central Europe, but sent a smaller force into Poland to keep the Poles from helping the Hungarians. Poland was then divided among several dukes of the Piast dynasty, who did not act together. The Mongols defeated the knights of Lesser Poland, among other places at Chmielnik in March 1241, and sacked Kraków.

Henry, who ruled Silesia and much of Lesser and Greater Poland and was the most powerful of the Polish dukes, gathered his army at Legnica. Besides Polish knights it included Teutonic Knights, Knights Templar and Hospitallers, foot soldiers and miners from the gold mines of the region, and the troops of his relative Duke Mieszko II the Fat of Opole. He was waiting for his brother-in-law, King Wenceslas I of Bohemia, who was approaching with an army, but chose to march out and fight before the Mongols could be reinforced. HistoryNet puts Henry's army at about 30,000 against some 20,000 Mongols; the Polish History portal says the Mongols were several times more numerous.

Henry drew up his army in four divisions, which went into battle one after another on the plain south-east of the town. Mongol archers did heavy damage, and a feigned flight drew the knights forward into a trap. A chronicle account, by Jan Długosz, tells of a Mongol banner that released foul-smelling smoke; HistoryNet describes smoke drifting between the infantry and the knights who had charged ahead, so that the Mongols could fall on the knights alone. Mieszko's men were the first to break. Henry charged with his own division and was killed; the Mongols cut off his head and showed it on a spear to the defenders of Legnica, who did not surrender. According to HistoryNet, the Templars died to a man.

Wenceslas, hearing of the defeat, withdrew. Two days later the main Mongol army crushed the Hungarians at Mohi, and the Mongols went on to ravage Silesia and Moravia, but Batu later turned back east on hearing of the death of his uncle and overlord, Ögedei. Poles long remembered 9 April as the day an Asian invasion was turned back; HistoryNet argues that the Mongol force in Poland had only ever been meant to protect the flank of the attack on Hungary. Henry's death also ended the chance of uniting Poland under the dukes of Silesia, whose lands were split among his heirs.

Q705874.title: Battle of Mohi
paras: The Battle of Mohi, also called the Battle of the Sajó River, was fought on 11 April 1241 in Hungary, about halfway between Pest and the kingdom's eastern border, between the army of King Béla IV of Hungary and the main Mongol invasion force under Batu Khan and his general Subutai. It was the turning point of the Mongol invasion of Hungary. The Mongols had driven the Cumans, or Qipchaqs, a nomadic people of the steppe, westwards; Béla had taken them into his kingdom in return for their conversion to Christianity, and Batu demanded that he give them up. While smaller Mongol forces raided Poland and other neighbouring lands to keep Hungary's allies away, Batu's main army broke through Hungary's eastern defences in March 1241.

Béla gathered his army at Pest, but it was weakened by quarrels: many nobles resented him, and after a mob killed the Cuman leader Koten on suspicion of treachery, the Cumans turned on the Hungarians and left. Béla then marched east and made contact with the Mongols in early April at the Sajó River, near the village of Mohi, where he held the main bridge and set up a camp ringed with wagons. Medievalists.net puts both armies at about 50,000 men; HistoryNet gives Béla 60,000-70,000 and calls the Mongol army larger.

Fighting began on the night of 10 April, when a Mongol attack on the bridge was beaten back by troops under Béla's brother Coloman and Archbishop Ugrin. Meanwhile Subutai led part of the Mongol army to a ford downstream, and around dawn on 11 April, as Batu's men forced the bridge with catapults and arrows, Subutai's force fell on the Hungarians from the rear. Surrounded and crowded in their camp, the Hungarians were bombarded with stones and fire. The Mongols then left a deliberate gap in their ring; the Hungarians streamed out through it, and the Mongol horsemen rode along the fleeing columns and cut them down. HistoryNet cites estimates of 40,000 to 65,000 dead; much of the kingdom's leadership was killed.

Béla escaped to Austria, where Duke Frederick held him until he gave up money and territory, and then fled to the Adriatic coast, pursued by the Mongols, and found refuge on an island near Trau (Trogir). With its army destroyed, Hungary could not organise a defence: the Mongols occupied the east of the kingdom in 1241 and crossed the Danube in the winter of 1242. In the spring of 1242 they withdrew, probably because Batu had learned of the death of the Mongol ruler Ögedei.

Q543165.title: Battle of Fort Sumter
paras: The bombardment of Fort Sumter, a federal fort in the harbour of Charleston, South Carolina, on 12-13 April 1861 was the opening engagement of the American Civil War. After Abraham Lincoln's election as president in 1860, South Carolina and six other Southern states seceded from the Union and formed the Confederate States of America. The seceding states seized most federal forts and property within their borders; Fort Sumter, held by a small U.S. Army garrison under Major Robert Anderson, was one of the few major posts the United States still held in the South.

Anderson had moved his men from Fort Moultrie, which could not be defended against attack by land, to the stronger Fort Sumter, but his supplies were running low, and a ship sent with reinforcements was driven off by fire from shore. Lincoln, who in his inaugural address had called secession unconstitutional, decided to try to resupply the fort. The Confederate government ordered Brigadier General P. G. T. Beauregard, commanding at Charleston, to demand the fort's evacuation and, if refused, to reduce it; Anderson refused.

At 4:30 a.m. on 12 April the Confederate batteries ringing the harbour opened fire. The garrison could not reply effectively. Fires broke out inside the fort, and at 2:30 p.m. on 13 April Anderson surrendered, after about 34 hours of bombardment (the American Battlefield Trust says nearly 36). He was allowed to leave with the honours of war and evacuated the fort the next day; according to the Trust, the only deaths came when a round exploded during his 100-gun salute to the flag, killing Private Daniel Hough and mortally wounding another soldier. Anderson's men sailed to New York, where they were greeted as heroes.

The North and the South at once called for volunteers to mobilise for war. The Confederates kept Fort Sumter for the rest of the war, withstanding a Union siege, from 1863 to 1865 according to the National Archives, that reduced most of it to rubble.

Q221469.title: First Battle of Bull Run
paras: The First Battle of Bull Run (also called First Manassas), fought on 21 July 1861 along the Bull Run creek near Manassas, Virginia, about 25 miles from Washington, was the first major land battle of the American Civil War. Under public pressure to take the Confederate capital, Richmond, quickly, Lincoln pressed the Union commander Brigadier General Irvin McDowell to advance. McDowell's army of 90-day volunteers, enthusiastic but barely trained, left Washington on 16 July. Facing it behind Bull Run was a Confederate army under Brigadier General P. G. T. Beauregard, as green as its opponents, guarding the railway junction at Manassas, which linked the Shenandoah Valley with the Virginia interior.

McDowell hoped to beat Beauregard before a second Confederate army under General Joseph E. Johnston could come from the Shenandoah Valley. But Johnston slipped away from the Union force watching him, and his men travelled to Manassas by train, arriving on 20 July; the Oxford Companion to American Military History calls this the first operational use of railways in war. On the morning of 21 July McDowell made a feint at the stone bridge over Bull Run while two divisions crossed upstream at Sudley Ford to turn the Confederate left. The Federals drove the Confederates back from Matthews Hill, but the defenders rallied on Henry Hill around a brigade of Virginians under Brigadier General Thomas J. Jackson. Brigadier General Barnard Bee, rallying his own men, pointed to Jackson 'standing like a stone wall', and Jackson was known as 'Stonewall' from then on.

Through the afternoon the Federals made piecemeal attacks on Henry Hill without breaking through. Around 4 p.m. fresh Confederate troops under Colonel Jubal Early and Brigadier General E. Kirby Smith struck the Union right; the Union line gave way and the withdrawal turned into a panicky retreat to Washington, slowed by civilian spectators who had come out from the capital to watch. The Confederates were too disorganised to pursue. According to the Oxford Companion, the Union lost 2,896 men and the Confederates 1,982.

The defeat ended Northern hopes of a short war. McDowell was relieved and replaced by Major General George B. McClellan, who reorganised and trained the force that became the Army of the Potomac. Northerners learned that enthusiasm alone would not win the war, while the victory strengthened Southern belief in their own fighting superiority.

Q719252.title: Battle of Antietam
paras: The Battle of Antietam, fought on 17 September 1862 near Sharpsburg, Maryland, between General Robert E. Lee's Confederate Army of Northern Virginia and Major General George B. McClellan's Union Army of the Potomac, was the deadliest single day in American history. After a summer of victories that had pushed the fighting in Virginia back from Richmond to the outskirts of Washington, Lee crossed the Potomac into Maryland in early September 1862, the first Confederate invasion of Union territory. He hoped for a victory that might bring British and French recognition of the Confederacy, help Northern opponents of the war in the coming congressional elections and push the Lincoln administration towards peace. Lincoln, for his part, had decided in July to proclaim the freeing of slaves in the rebel states and was waiting for a Union victory to announce it.

Lee divided his army, sending three parts under Stonewall Jackson to capture the Union garrison at Harpers Ferry. Union soldiers at Frederick then found a lost copy of Lee's orders, but McClellan moved slowly: he forced the South Mountain passes but could not save Harpers Ferry, which surrendered to Jackson. Lee gathered most of his army on high ground near Sharpsburg behind Antietam Creek. McClellan had about 80,000 men to Lee's 45,000, according to the Oxford Companion to American Military History, yet believed himself outnumbered.

At dawn on 17 September Joseph Hooker's corps attacked Lee's left, and the fighting surged back and forth through the Cornfield, the West Woods and around the Dunker Church, where Jackson's men held. Around midday two Union divisions broke through the Confederate centre along a sunken farm road, later called Bloody Lane, but McClellan did not follow up. In the afternoon Ambrose Burnside's corps finally forced its way across a stone bridge over the creek and advanced towards Sharpsburg, threatening Lee's line of retreat, until A. P. Hill's division arrived after a forced march from Harpers Ferry and struck its flank. Because the Union attacks came one after another rather than together, Lee could shift troops to each threatened point, and McClellan never committed his whole army.

Some 6,000 men were dead or dying and about 16,000 wounded, more than 22,000 casualties in all. Lee withdrew across the Potomac into Virginia after 18 September, and McClellan did not pursue him effectively; Lincoln later replaced him with Burnside. Although the battle was tactically a draw, it ended Lee's invasion. Five days later, on 22 September, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, declaring free the slaves of all states still in rebellion on 1 January 1863. Britain and France did not recognise the Confederacy, and the Republicans kept control of the House of Representatives in November.

Q745979.title: Battle of Chancellorsville
paras: The Battle of Chancellorsville, fought from 30 April to 6 May 1863 in the Wilderness of central Virginia, is considered General Robert E. Lee's greatest victory. After the Union defeat at Fredericksburg, Lincoln gave command of the Army of the Potomac to Major General Joseph Hooker, who rebuilt its morale and planned a spring campaign to turn the left flank of Lee's Army of Northern Virginia at Fredericksburg. Hooker had about 130,000 men; Lee, with James Longstreet's corps away on a supply mission, had about 60,000. At the end of April Hooker left John Sedgwick with some 40,000 men opposite Fredericksburg and led the rest across the Rappahannock River into the dense woods of the Wilderness, around the Chancellorsville crossroads.

Lee did not retreat. Leaving Jubal Early's division to watch Sedgwick, he moved the rest of his army west against Hooker. On 1 May the two sides clashed in the woods, and Hooker halted his advance and pulled back to a defensive position at Chancellorsville. That evening Lee and Stonewall Jackson planned a bold stroke: on 2 May Jackson led about 28,000-30,000 men on a long march across the front of the Union army to its open right flank, while Lee held Hooker's attention with some 15,000. Warnings of the flank march were ignored at Hooker's headquarters, where it was taken as a sign that Lee was retreating.

At about 5 p.m. Jackson's men burst out of the thickets, overran Oliver O. Howard's XI Corps and rolled up the Union line. That night, riding ahead of his lines in the dark, Jackson was mistaken for Union cavalry and shot by men of a North Carolina regiment; he was mortally wounded, and J. E. B. Stuart took over his corps. On 3 May the Confederates renewed the attack in heavy fighting around the crossroads; Hooker gave up key ground and was knocked senseless when a shell struck a pillar he was leaning on. The same day Sedgwick broke through Early at Fredericksburg, but Lee divided his army yet again, stopped Sedgwick at Salem Church and forced him back across the river.

Although Hooker, after some 17,000 casualties by the Oxford Companion's count, still outnumbered Lee two to one, he decided to retreat, and the Army of the Potomac recrossed the Rappahannock on 5-6 May. The victory was costly for the South, above all in the loss of Jackson. Buoyed by it, Lee invaded Pennsylvania, leading to the Battle of Gettysburg in July 1863.

Q154942.title: Battle of Königgrätz
paras: The Battle of Königgrätz, also called Sadowa after a nearby village, was fought on 3 July 1866 in Bohemia, near the fortress town of Königgrätz (Hradec Králové) on the Elbe, and decided the Austro-Prussian or Seven Weeks' War over leadership of the German states. Prussia, whose army was directed by its chief of staff Helmuth von Moltke, faced Austria's North Army under General Ludwig von Benedek, together with Saxon troops. After a run of defeats in Bohemia, Benedek withdrew to a position between the Bistritz river and the Elbe, with his back to the Elbe.

Moltke had sent three widely separated armies into Bohemia to converge on the Austrians. His plan for the battle was for the First Army to pin Benedek in front, for the Army of the Elbe to turn the Austrian left, held by the Saxons, and for the Second Army under Crown Prince Frederick William to strike the exposed Austrian right. EBSCO's account puts Benedek's force at about 195,000 Austrians and 25,000 Saxons, and the Prussian armies at about 140,000 and 115,000. According to the same account, the Second Army was still some twenty miles away when the fighting began on the morning of 3 July.

The Prussian First Army's advance across the Bistritz suffered badly from the more accurate Austrian rifled artillery, while the Austrians, attacking in dense columns, were cut down by the Prussian breech-loading 'needle guns', which fired much faster than their muzzle-loaders. In the Swiepwald wood a single Prussian division under Eduard von Fransecky held off much larger Austrian forces all day. Benedek did not launch a general attack while he had the chance, and around midday the Second Army began to arrive on his right flank, taking the key villages of Lipa and Chlum, while the Saxons on the left were outflanked. Austrian counter-attacks on Chlum failed, and in the afternoon the Austrian army began to break up and flee towards the Elbe bridges; only a fighting retreat covered by the Austrian artillery kept the defeat from becoming a complete rout.

EBSCO's two accounts put Prussian losses at about 9,000 and Austrian losses at about 25,000 killed and wounded and 20,000 prisoners, or about 43,000 in all with about half captured, plus some 1,500 Saxons. Emperor Franz Joseph gave up the war, which was ended by the Peace of Prague later that summer. Austria was excluded from German affairs and from the new North German Confederation led by Prussia, a decisive step towards German unification under Prussia in 1871. The battle also showed the power of breech-loading rifles and of Moltke's method of fast-converging separate armies, which Prussia used again against France in 1870.
